title: Sharding: when it becomes unavoidable, and what it costs forever

videos.script: Everything in this course so far made one server do more. {{one-server}} This lesson is about giving that up. Sharding splits one table's rows across several servers, each holding a part and none holding the whole. {{split}} It is the last resort, and the lesson starts by saying why. Reads can be spread over copies. Writes cannot, because every copy needs every write. So sharding is for the day the writes alone outgrow the biggest machine you can buy. {{wall}} Before that day there is a long list to try, and most databases never get past it. {{list}} Then the decision you cannot take back: which column decides where a row lives. In the course's shop, one seller has a quarter of all orders. Split by seller, one server gets almost half the load. {{hot}} Next you build two shards on your own machine, and watch the queries. One that names the key goes to one shard. One that does not goes to all of them. A total across every shard pulls two million rows over the wire. {{wire}} And three things a single server did for you stop working. A unique id. A join. A transaction, which commits on one shard and fails on the other. {{breaks}} Last, the bill that keeps coming: moving rows, changing schemas, backups and ids. {{bill}}
